clue.text: Upheavals from changes in posture

indicators.note: changes tells us the letters of the words that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some seismic event or social upheaval is put down to people shifting their posture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges the nine letters of IN POSTURE; 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Volcanic outbursts and sudden violent disturbances are both called upheavals.

clue.text: No crowding in chamber for Katisha's joint admirers?

parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado, Katisha boasts that people come miles to admire her right elbow
a chamber is a room

explanation.surface: A Gilbert and Sullivan joke: a room for the fans of Katisha's famous elbow.
explanation.walkthrough: Katisha, in The Mikado, has an elbow people travel to see, so a chamber for its admirers is an elbow room; 'in', 'for' and 'admirers' dress the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Having space to move freely means there is no crowding.

clue.text: --, Eros; the long day's task is done" (A & C)

definitions.text: --, Eros; the long day's task is done" (A & C)

parts.words: --, Eros; the long day's task is done" (A & C)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from Antony and Cleopatra: Antony tells his servant Eros to take off his armour

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra with its first word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word opens Antony's line in Act IV of Antony and Cleopatra (A & C), where he asks Eros to strip off his armour.
explanation.definitionFit: To disarm or take off armour is the old verb Antony uses, so it fills the blank in the quotation.

clue.text: Editor after a story isn't half gifted

indicators.note: after places the editor's abbreviation at the end

parts.note: a story is a tale

indicators.note: isn't half means only the second half of the word isn't is used

explanation.surface: A cheeky aside that an editor following a story is really rather gifted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'isn't half' looks like the British phrase meaning 'very', but it takes the back half of the word; 'after' sends the editor to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone gifted has natural ability, the same thing as having talent.

clue.text: Concerning a terrible pest, go too far

parts.note: over can mean about or concerning, as in a row over money

indicators.note: terrible tells us the letters of pest are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone reacting to a dreadful pest is warned not to overreact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' rearranges PEST into STEP; 'a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To exceed a limit or boundary is to go too far.

clue.text: A fine candlestick

explanation.surface: A two-word note praising the quality of a candlestick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A fine' reads as an adjective praising the candlestick, but it is a penalty, the Oxford college forfeit.
explanation.definitionFit: At Oxford colleges a forfeit imposed at dinner had the old name for a penalty; it is also a wall bracket holding candles.

clue.text: Carrier of Kipling's ugly lump

parts.note: Kipling's Just So Story tells how a lazy desert beast got a hump on its back as punishment

explanation.surface: Someone bearing an unsightly lump described by Rudyard Kipling.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's Just So Stories include How the ___ Got His Hump; the beast of burden carries that 'ugly lump'.
explanation.definitionFit: The desert animal carries its hump, given to it in Kipling's tale for idleness.

clue.text: Turn the point over to settle it

explanation.surface: Advice to flip a nail's point so as to finish a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Bending the protruding tip of a nail flat is to rivet it this way; to settle a deal decisively is to seal it the same way.

clue.text: Could one so describe an ally — more in alarm, perhaps?

definitions.text: Could one so describe an ally

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of more and alarm may be arranged in another way

explanation.surface: A playful question whether a friend could be called this, judging by rising alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: An ally (or alley) is a playing marble, so it could be called marble-like; 'perhaps' rearranges MORE and ALARM together, with 'in' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means made of or like marble, and an ally is a child's marble.

clue.text: Send off without a meal

indicators.note: without tells us a letter is dropped from the word for send off

parts.note: to launch a ship or rocket is to send it off

explanation.surface: Someone is dispatched without being fed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without a' removes A from LAUNCH; 'meal' at the end is the definition, not part of the hungry send-off.
explanation.definitionFit: The midday meal is the one commonly eaten around noon.

clue.text: Characters some have at their fingertips …

definitions.text: Characters some have at their fingertips …

parts.words: Characters some have at their fingertips
parts.note: letters that a blind reader literally feels with the fingertips, punning on knowing something by heart

explanation.surface: People who know the alphabet so well they have it at their fingertips.
explanation.walkthrough: To have something at your fingertips is to know it well; here the raised dot characters are read by touch.
explanation.definitionFit: The raised-dot writing system for blind people is read by touching its characters.

clue.text: …or a Greek one that means nothing to us

definitions.text: …or a Greek one that means nothing to us

parts.words: or a Greek one that means nothing to us
parts.note: continuing 9 across, a Greek character whose shape, a round O, looks like zero to English readers

explanation.surface: A Greek character that conveys nothing to English readers.
explanation.walkthrough: Following 9 across, 'one' is a character; the Greek short o looks like our O, which also stands for zero, 'nothing'.
explanation.definitionFit: This Greek letter is the round short o, shaped like a nought.

clue.text: Marches (four) were little ones

parts.note: the four March sisters are heroines of Louisa May Alcott's novel Little ___

explanation.surface: Something about four marches being small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marches' reads as walking or borderlands, but it is the surname of Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy in Alcott's Little ___.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcott's novel calls the four March girls little ladies, giving its title.

clue.text: Half the prescribed outfit for lamentations

definitions.text: Half the prescribed outfit for lamentations

parts.words: Half the prescribed outfit for lamentations
parts.note: the Biblical mourning costume is a pairing of coarse fabric and ashes, so this is one of its two halves

explanation.surface: A mourner's dress code, of which only half is given.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'in ___ and ashes' describes Biblical mourning or penance; this is the first half.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse fabric worn in mourning or penance is half of the set phrase with ashes.

clue.text: Lids up, surprised

explanation.surface: Someone raises their eyelids in astonishment.
explanation.definitionFit: With eyelids raised you are wide awake and alert; astonished people stare wide-eyed too.

clue.text: Recipe Una cooked for Marius

indicators.note: cooked suggests the letters of recipe and Una are mixed up like ingredients

explanation.surface: Una follows a recipe to make something for her friend Marius.
explanation.walkthrough: Walter Pater's novel is Marius the ___, so the hero's name stands for the word; 'cooked' rearranges RECIPE and UNA, and 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter Pater's hero bears this label in the title of his novel, meaning a follower of pleasure-seeking philosophy.

clue.text: Old banger, a bargain, but no starter

definitions.note: a heap is slang for a decrepit old car, a banger in British English

indicators.note: no starter means the opening letter of the word for a bargain is dropped

parts.note: something that is a bargain is cheap

explanation.surface: An ancient car on sale for a song, though it won't start.
explanation.walkthrough: A banger is British slang for an old car. 'no starter' drops the C of CHEAP; a car with no starter is the surface joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A clapped-out motor is called a heap, short for a heap of junk.

clue.text: Pod worn by a sailor?

parts.note: a pod could be called the jacket of a pea, and seamen wear a short heavy coat of that name

explanation.surface: A seaman wearing a seed pod.
explanation.walkthrough: A pod is a pea's jacket; the sailor's short woollen coat has the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors wear a short double-breasted woollen coat of this name.

clue.text: A treatise that's not bound to be read

definitions.text: A treatise that's not bound to be read

parts.words: A treatise that's not bound to be read
parts.note: a short tract issued unbound, with a pun on not being obliged to be read

explanation.surface: An essay nobody is obliged to read.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not bound' reads as 'not obliged', but means without a hard binding.
explanation.definitionFit: A short unbound booklet arguing a case is a small tract.

clue.text: Has the defence department moved to Penang?

indicators.note: moved says the letters of to and Penang have been shifted around

explanation.surface: Has the US military headquarters relocated to Penang in Malaysia?
explanation.walkthrough: 'moved' rearranges TO PENANG; 'Has the' is a link. Penang is a Malaysian island state.
explanation.definitionFit: The five-sided building in Virginia houses the US Department of Defense and names it.

clue.text: Chief shows strength

explanation.surface: A leader displays power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows' links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Chief means principal, and strength is the old sense kept in 'with might and ___'.

clue.text: 6 ac with back trouble is in bed

parts.note: the answer to 6 across, the humped beast

indicators.note: back tells us the word for trouble is turned round

parts.note: to ail is to trouble

explanation.surface: A humped animal with a bad back is laid up in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns AIL into LIA; 'is in bed' looks like illness but is a shrub planted in a flower bed.
explanation.definitionFit: This flowering shrub grows in garden beds.

clue.text: He screens the screenings

parts.note: an official who vets films shown in cinemas, screening in the sense of filtering

explanation.surface: A projectionist showing films.
explanation.walkthrough: 'screens' means filters out, while 'screenings' are film showings.
explanation.definitionFit: An official who examines films and cuts objectionable material filters what is shown.

clue.text: Slips of slips

parts.note: a list of mistakes printed on a separate sheet of paper in a book

explanation.surface: Two kinds of slip.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Slips' is the sheets of paper, the second the mistakes they list.
explanation.definitionFit: A printed list of misprints inserted into a book records mistakes.

clue.text: Long-lasting cheese

parts.note: Agatha Christie's play has run in London since 1952, and cheap cheese is jokingly given its name as bait

explanation.surface: A cheese that keeps well.
explanation.walkthrough: Agatha Christie's play has run in London's West End since 1952; cheap cheddar fit only for baiting traps is nicknamed after the same device.
explanation.definitionFit: Christie's record-running play bears this name, as does cheap cheese fit only for baiting.

clue.text: Muslim lawyer in civvies

explanation.surface: An Islamic jurist dressed in ordinary clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in civvies' is the phrase 'in ___': civilian dress; 'in' links.
explanation.definitionFit: An expert in Islamic law has this title, and plain clothes worn by an off-duty soldier are called by the same word.

clue.text: Head-dress in Major Barbara — it's coming back

indicators.note: coming back says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the letters sit inside the words of the title that follows

parts.note: the title of Shaw's play followed by it's, with the letters running across the word break

explanation.surface: A reference to a head-dress in Shaw's play Major Barbara.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Head-dress in Major' as the definition, but 'in' is the hidden-word signal; the jewelled head-dress is just 'Head-dress'. 'coming back' reverses ARAIT from BarbARA IT's.
explanation.definitionFit: A jewelled ornamental crown worn on the head is a head-dress.

clue.text: Fragrance that may drift from the sound of it

indicators.note: from the sound of it says the word is what we hear spoken

parts.note: one who may drift is a wanderer, a roamer

explanation.surface: A scent might waft away, by the sound of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drift' suggests the scent wafting, but it is 'a roamer', a drifter, spoken in a non-rhotic British accent.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleasant smell or scent is a fragrance.

clue.text: Flower said to give you arctic feeling?

indicators.note: said tells us the word is heard spoken

parts.note: to make you feel icy cold is to freeze you, colloquially freeze ya

explanation.surface: A bloom said to chill the recipient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freeze ya' (freeze you) said aloud gives the flower's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A fragrant South African plant of the iris family grown for cut flowers.

clue.text: A record — for lumberjack might one think?

parts.note: a woodcutter might suppose a volume about timber suits him

explanation.surface: Lumberjacks musing that a ship's record is meant for them.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan prints 'lumberjacks'. A ship's journal looks to a woodcutter like a book about logs.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's or vehicle's journal records journeys and events.

clue.text: Bull ring enclosure

parts.note: on an archery or darts target, the ring that encloses the bullseye

explanation.surface: A pen in a bullfighting arena.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bull ring' suggests the arena, but it is the bullseye on a target, enclosed by the next ring out.
explanation.definitionFit: On a target the ring surrounding the bullseye is the one nearest the centre.

clue.text: Waiting on the server

explanation.surface: Waiting for the waiter.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means accompanying or ministering to; as a noun a servant or steward who serves.
